newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Rhone-Poulenc first half up 14 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rhone-Poulenc first half up 14 pct.

text.p: French chemicals and pharmaceuticals company Rhone-Poulenc SA reported a 14 percent increase in its first half profits on Friday and maintained its forecast of a 20 percent full-year rise.

Investors and analysts welcomed the figures, which came in at the high end of expectations, and the share opened 3.4 percent higher. At 0913 GMT, Rhone was 2.66 percent higher at 255.10 francs while the CAC-40 index of blue-chip shares was up 0.98 percent.
Rhone-Poulenc said its second quarter net income rose by 20.2 percent to 934 million francs ($151.1 million) , adding up to a first half profit of 1.608 billion, up 14 percent.
Sales were 8.5 percent higher in the second quarter to 23.435 billion francs and 7.5 percent to 45.034 billion for the first half, benefiting from a higher dollar.
"The second quarter has confirmed the continued growth in the Group's results," Chairman Jean-Rene Fourtou said in a statement.
"We are therefore maintaining our objective of increasing earnings per share by 20 percent in 1997, excluding exceptional items," he added.

The pharmaceuticals sector, mainly the 68.3 percent subsidiary Rhone-Poulenc Rorer Inc, had a 9.7 percent drop in its profit contribution to 1.861 billion francs. This was mainly due to the impact of a product recall at the Centeon joint-venture of Rorer and Germany's Hoechst.
Rhone said that excluding the Centeon impact, the earnings in the sector would have increased by 20.1 percent.
Rhone said that new pharmaceutical products such as Taxotere, Granocyte and Lovenox were behind the rise.

In Animal and Plant Health there was a 6.9 percent increase in the first half profit contribution to 1.737 billion francs while chemicals posted a 16.9 percent increase to 727 million francs partly due to lower provisions for restructuring.
At Fibers & Polymers there was a 187.5 percent rise to 207 million, mainly reflecting a very poor 1996 comparison.

Managing director Igor Landau told Reuters that while the dollar rise helped sales in the first half it had not contributed much to earnings because the company had at the start of the year covered its exchange rate exposure.
"What I feel is that we do not see a lot of the plus of the dollar in terms of operating result yet," Landau said in a telephone interview, adding this would be more important in the second half.
On June 26, Rhone-Poulenc said that it planned to make a 25 billion franc buy-out bid on minorities in Rhone-Poulenc Rorer after a standstill agreement expires on July 31.

The share price in Rorer has risen since from $79 to more than $93. Rhone had suggested a price of $92 per share. "I re-affirm today that we feel the price of $92 is an attractive price to the shareholders," Landau said.
He said that Rhone was awaiting the outcome of a study by a special Rorer committee and also a discussion with the Rorer board before making its next move.
Landau said that the company's five billion franc asset sale programme was going as planned.

"At the end of the first half, one billion has been booked. Almost all assets that we plan to divest are in negotiation and it is very difficult to tell you what is going to fall in 1997 and what in 1998 because these things take time," he said.
The sale programme is independent of Rhone-Poulenc's plan to merge its Fibres & Polymers sector with its Chemicals sector into a separate company in which it will retain a majority stake.
"Whatever happens, we are going to make this fibres and chemicals merger in a separate company and we are going to put it on the (share) market, if the market permits it, in early 1998," Landau said.
Financial analysts said they were pleased with the results. "It was a pleasant surprise," said Hans Zuyd of Paribas in London.

"We were expecting 1.55 billion, so (the first half net income at 1.608 billion) was slightly higher. It is always nice to see that a higher range has been met, especially when you see the improvements in the chemicals and fibres sectors, they seem to be doing quite well there," Zuyd said.
Brokerage Ferri in Paris raised its 1997 net income forecast to 3.425 billion francs from 3.325 billion for a 24 percent rise over the 1996 figure. ($ = 6.179 French Francs)
